name: The Flat Arch That Is Actually Flat
symptom: A gauged or jack arch over a masonry opening is set dead level on its soffit. Within a few years, and often immediately, it reads as sagging in the middle, because the eye reads a long horizontal line above a void as bowing downward even when it is straight. On a wide opening the effect is pronounced; on a 6 ft opening it is the difference between an arch that looks confident and one that looks tired.

cause.explanation: A flat arch is drawn as a rectangle in every drawing package and dimensioned to a level soffit, because the camber is a fraction of an inch and would not survive a dimension string. The mason then works to a level string line, which is the correct instinct for every other course in the wall. The camber is a piece of craft knowledge that lives in the setting-out and not in the documents, so it disappears the moment the work is drawn rather than laid out on a rod.
cause.cost_saved: None. A cambered template costs the same as a level one. The camber is lost to notation, not to money.

rule_violated.statement: camber = opening_width / 96, which is 3/8 in on a 36 in opening and 3/4 in on a 6 ft one. A flat arch is not flat: it is cambered so it does not read as sagging.

The same correction that makes a stylobate crown and an entasis swell applies at every long horizontal read against a void. The correction is not decoration; without it the element reports a failure that has not occurred.

correct_practice: Rise the soffit of a flat arch by opening width / 96 at the centre, about 1 in 96 or 0.6 degrees, struck from a very long radius or set out as a shallow segment. The skewback should be set at about 60 degrees for a gauged arch and the joints must radiate from a common centre, which means the voussoirs are tapered and the joints are not parallel — a jack arch with parallel joints is a lintel with lines drawn on it. Where the arch is segmental instead, rise = opening width / 8, that is 4 1/2 in on a 36 in opening. Arch depth about one module — four brick courses — so the arch reads as a member and not as a soldier course.

fixes.right: Camber the soffit at 1 in 96 and radiate the joints from a struck centre. Set out full size on a rod before laying.
fixes.cheap: If the arch must be laid level, deepen it: an arch four or five courses deep reads as substantial enough that the eye stops looking for the sag. Alternatively use a segmental arch, whose rise is unmistakable and which is cheaper to build than a gauged flat arch anyway.
fixes.dishonest: A precast or cut-stone lintel scored with false joint lines. The joints will be parallel rather than radiating, which is the giveaway, and the piece will show a single continuous shrinkage or weathering pattern across what is meant to be nine separate stones.

detection: Sight along the soffit of the arch in a rectified frontal photograph and compare its centre with its ends: a correct arch is 3/8 to 3/4 in higher in the middle, which at typical photograph resolution is one or two pixels of the opening width — about 1 per cent. Easier and more diagnostic: look at the joints. Radiating joints, wider at the top than at the soffit, mean a real arch; parallel vertical joints mean a soldier course or a scored lintel. Third: check the depth against the brick courses. A one-course-deep soldier over a 6 ft opening is not an arch.

exceptions.why: The style deliberately uses a plain rectangular stone lintel with no arch action expressed at all, and a Greek Revival head is honestly a beam.
exceptions.bounds: It must be a stone or timber lintel and must look like one: a single member, full width, with visible bearing at each end and no false joints. A brick soldier course pretending to be a lintel is not this.

bounds_test.note: It must be a stone or timber lintel and must look like one: a single member, full width, with visible bearing at each end and no false joints. A brick soldier course pretending to be a lintel scores above 1 and is not this.

granted_when.note: Depends on the head genuinely being a beam.

exceptions.why: A continuous lintel course running unbroken around the building is the point; individual arches would break it.
exceptions.bounds: The course must be continuous and must return around every corner.

bounds_test.note: The course must be continuous and must return around every corner.

exceptions.why: Openings are headed by timber lintels in a mud-plastered wall and no arch exists in the tradition.
exceptions.bounds: Timber lintel expressed or concealed in stucco, with a minimum 10 in reveal. No arched or keystoned head anywhere on the building.

bounds_test.note: Timber lintel expressed or concealed in stucco with a minimum 10 in reveal, and no arched or keystoned head anywhere on the building.

granted_when.note: Depends on the wall expressing thickness; a 2 in stucco skin over frame voids it.

confused_with.difference: That fault is about an arch that is not carrying anything. This one is about an arch that is carrying and does not look like it.

That fault is an arch shape over a veneer whose span is carried by a steel angle. This one is a real arch, or a real lintel, built without its optical correction. The joint-radiation test distinguishes them: that fault often has radiating joints and no load, this one has load and no camber.

sources: Brick Industry Association Technical Note 31, brick masonry arches
Measured gauged arches, mid-Atlantic and Tidewater 1700-1800

test.note: THE PHOTOGRAPHIC TEST, and not the one the fault is named for. Radiating joints, wider at the top than at the soffit, mean a real arch; parallel joints mean a soldier course or a scored lintel. The camber itself is about 1 per cent of the opening width and is at or below the resolution of a street photograph, so this is the check that can actually be run.

secondary_tests.note: The rule itself: camber = opening_width / 96, that is 3/8 in on a 36 in opening and 3/4 in on a 6 ft one, about 1 in 96 or 0.6 degrees. HONEST LIMIT: at 1 per cent of the opening this is one or two pixels in a typical elevation photograph and needs a rectified drawing or a string line on site.
Arch depth about one module, four courses. A one-course soldier over a 6 ft opening is not an arch, and depth is the variable that lets a level-laid arch stop reading as a sag.

severity_by_style.why: The style uses a plain rectangular stone or timber lintel with no arch action expressed, and a Greek Revival head is honestly a beam.
A continuous lintel course runs unbroken around the building; individual arches would break it.
Timber lintels in a mud-plastered wall; no arch exists in the tradition.
Where the wall is or fully expresses cut stone with true voussoirs, the optical correction is expected and its absence reads as a failure of the stonework.
